The island needs about 30–45 MB and stays there. The ceiling is a limit, not a target: raising it does not make anything faster, and the app will not grow to fill it. Earlier versions allocated real memory to meet the number on the dial, which was waste — that is gone. The reserve for Android is never touched.

The CPU figure is this app\'s own share of wall-clock time, not the system\'s. A live system-wide CPU percentage has not been readable by an ordinary app since /proc/stat was restricted in Android 8 — anything showing you one without root is a system app or is making it up.
A page inside the app. No internet connection is involved.

Dynamic Camera Punch is a system overlay that turns your punch-hole camera into a live island.

It contains no third-party libraries at all — no AndroidX, no Kotlin runtime, nothing. Every control in this app is drawn on a Canvas, which is why the whole thing fits in a couple of hundred kilobytes.

Six permissions, every one used. No QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES. No INTERNET — this app has never made a network request and cannot.

MIT licensed. Not affiliated with or endorsed by Apple.

Short, one-off things your phone does that the island can announce as it happens — plugging in, running low, switching to vibrate, connecting headphones.\n\nThese four need no permission at all. They work on a fresh install with nothing granted beyond the overlay itself, because Android broadcasts them to any app that asks to listen.
These work with no notification access. They are broadcast by the system, not read from your notifications.

Things that stay on the island while they are happening, rather than appearing and vanishing — a track playing, a call ringing, a timer counting down, a route step, a download filling up.\n\nAll of these are read from notifications, so they need notification access. Without it the island still works; it just has less to say.
Read from your notifications, so these need notification access. Turn one off and it stops reaching the island entirely.

What each touch on the island does. Every gesture can be set to anything, or to nothing.\n\nDouble tap is set to Nothing by default on purpose: with nothing bound to it, a single tap can act the moment you lift your finger. Bind it and every single tap has to wait ~300 ms to find out whether a second one is coming.
Assignments are stored by name, not by position in this list, so a future version adding an action cannot silently change what your gestures do.
Choose which apps reach the island, and how their notifications behave when they get there

Which apps are allowed to put something on the island, and what happens when they do.\n\nWith no apps picked, every app is allowed — an empty list would otherwise mean an island that never appears, which reads as broken. Add your first app and the list becomes a filter.
Whether an arriving notification opens itself or waits to be tapped
How long an alert stays up before it collapses on its own
Clear a notification from the shade once the island has shown it

Two limits worth knowing: the brief banner at the top of the screen still appears, because the system has already posted the notification before any app is told about it — no app can suppress that. And clearing is the same as swiping it away, so the island becomes the only place that notification was ever shown. Ongoing notifications are never touched.
